 Food and beverage manufacturers, alongside grocery store groups, are urging the Trump administration to rethink a policy banning federal aid recipients in 18 states from buying soda and candy with their benefits.
 Several stakeholders questioned the US Agriculture Department’s legal authority to block the spending of Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits on certain sugary or processed products.
 Comments submitted to the agency in October by food companies and retailers that stand to lose business under the policy could preview future litigation against the administration.
 “I would highly anticipate additional legal challenges will be filed,” said Stewart Fried, an attorney who advises SNAP retailers in states that restricted purchases.
 States with bans approved by the department account for 11.1 million of 36.1 million program participants, according to USDA data published in October.
 Yet federal officials appear unlikely to back down barring a court order, with Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins touting the policy as one of the most concrete wins for the administration’s Make America Healthy Again agenda. On Oct. 30, USDA alerted grocers in four states that restrictions were taking effect the next day.
 The USDA has broad authority to greenlight projects that test program changes under the Food and Nutrition Act, an agency spokesperson said in an emailed statement.
 ‘The political landscape has shifted’
 The pressure comes as political factors could also stymie the restrictions, which have been largely backed by Republican leadership, in four states where Democrats gained control of governorships after the Nov. 3 midterm elections: Iowa, Nevada, Ohio, and Texas.
 Except for Nevada, those states passed laws seeking the restrictions.
 Fried said he wouldn’t be surprised if retailers lobbied newly elected governors and legislators to rescind the restrictions, which a state can only implement with USDA’s approval.
 Nevada Gov.-elect Aaron Ford (D) has fought the Trump administration on SNAP policy before — he was among the 21 state attorneys general who sued federal officials in November 2025 for withholding SNAP benefits during a government shutdown.
 Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa (D), on the other hand, voted in support of purchase restrictions as a state legislator.
 None of the incoming governors made public comments on the policy during their campaigns, and their spokespeople didn’t return requests for comment.
 To be sure, a state’s political leadership isn’t a surefire predictor of the policy’s future. Though Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger (D) supported broadening the foods eligible for purchase under SNAP while serving in Congress, purchase restrictions her Republican predecessor sought took effect Nov. 1.
 “In one of these states where the political landscape has shifted, if the people in charge now feel differently about this, they can just stop,” Katharine Deabler-Meadows, a senior attorney at the National Center for Law and Economic Justice, said in an interview.
 The center is representing SNAP recipients in a lawsuit that in June convinced a federal judge to vacate the restrictions in Colorado, Iowa, Nebraska, Tennessee, and West Virginia. The USDA appealed that decision in August.
 Fried said he expects “parallel challenges during the pending appeal,” given the decision only applied to the five states the litigation involved. 
 Colorado, one of two states where Democratic governors pursued the waivers, abandoned the effort Oct. 12, noting “federal policy currently prohibits states from piloting programs that restrict SNAP food and beverage purchases.”
 Nebraska is the only one of the five states whose restrictions were vacated that’s resubmitted a proposal the USDA is reviewing. Health officials in Iowa, Tennessee, and West Virginia didn’t reply to requests for comment on whether they would continue pursuing the policy.
 Colorado Department of Human Services spokesperson John Rosa said in an emailed statement state officials are “evaluating its next steps and tracking how peer states like Nebraska are proceeding” after the court ruling.
 ‘Log on the fire’ 
 Several policy opponents cited that June federal court ruling vacating restrictions in five states as a core reason the government shouldn’t continue approving restrictions or start enforcing them.
 “The waiver relies on the same authority the court said USDA cannot use for projects like this one,” the American Beverage Association said in an October letter addressing Texas’ proposed pilot. The group represents beverage companies including Coca-Cola Co. and PepsiCo Inc. 
 Chobani and Ocean Spray , companies that respectively sell yogurt and cranberry products, warned in comment letters that overly broad restrictions risk ensnaring foods with health benefits.
 While the restrictions limit sales of certain products, the consequences for a noncompliant retailer are even more severe: USDA can bar them from accepting SNAP benefits at the register.
 “The loss of SNAP authorization can have significant consequences for communities that rely on a local retailer like Casey’s as an accessible source of food,” Casey’s General Stores Inc. , the third-largest convenience store chain in the country, wrote to USDA.
 Casey’s warned efforts to avoid that consequence required significant compliance investment to update point-of-sale systems and train employees. The Food Industry Association, which represents companies at several levels of the US food supply chain, urged USDA to vacate its restrictions. It has estimated complying with the policy will cost food retailers about $1.6 billion initially and $759 million annually.
 Cindy Long, a former administrator of the SNAP program and deputy undersecretary overseeing all USDA nutrition programs, said outlining specific legal concerns at the comment stage that later reappeared in litigation was a common phenomenon.
 If USDA “goes out and starts disqualifying retailers, that’s another log on the fire that might tilt someone’s calculation about whether they take legal action,” Long said.
 The aforementioned companies and groups declined or didn’t respond to requests for comment on possible litigation challenging the restrictions.
 As circuit judges and fresh political leaders consider the policy anew, SNAP shoppers are already experiencing the change. Purchases of restricted beverages including soda and energy drinks dropped by 12% during the first half of 2026 in SNAP households, according to early research .
